statement: In the 50 US states and the District of Columbia from 2018 to 2022, a state law making fentanyl test strips legal (16 jurisdictions with a dated law, from June 2018 to August 2022), compared with the same states before their law and with states that had no such law at the time, is associated with fewer deaths from drug overdose than the comparison predicted, in one state-level study (Bhai et al., 2025; no funding, no conflicts declared): about 7% fewer per 100,000 residents (6.7%, 95% CI 1.4% to 11.7%, without adjustment; 7.1%, 3.4% to 10.7%, adjusted for age, rurality and income; editors' calculation from the reported coefficients), which at the death rate in state-months with a law is roughly 2.6 to 2.8 fewer deaths per 100,000 residents a year (editors' rough calculation). With adjustment the figures were similar for White (8.0%) and Black residents (8.4%); the abstract's 13.5% for Black residents is the unadjusted estimate (11.9%) converted with its sign reversed. Unintentional overdose deaths, set against overdose deaths by suicide, homicide or undetermined intent, were 5% to 8% lower, with weak support without adjustment and no difference for Black residents with adjustment (−0.2%; 95% CI −5.2% to +5.0%). This is a study of laws in whole state populations, not of people who used strips: it can show that death rates in these states ran below the comparison after their laws, but not that the laws or the strips caused it, nor whether people who tested their drugs were less likely to die. It did not measure whether strips were handed out or used, it counted deaths from any drug rather than opioid or fentanyl deaths, and it did not allow for other state policies or for changes in each state's drug supply at the same time; a 2026 correction says the authors modified some of the legal dates taken from their source and documented this in an online appendix not read here, and six states that the paper's map shows as legal have no date in its table. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one study of US states from 2018 to 2022, drug deaths were about 7 in 100 lower after a state made fentanyl test strips legal than the trends in other states predicted: roughly 3 fewer deaths a year for every 100,000 people. Results were about the same for White and Black residents once age, rural living and income were allowed for. The study looked at laws and death records, not at people using strips. It did not check whether more strips were handed out or used, it counted deaths from any drug, and other changes at the same time could explain the difference. A later correction says the authors changed some of the law dates from their source.
population: All residents of the 50 US states and the District of Columbia, 2018 to 2022, counted through state-by-month death and population records; White and Black residents also analysed separately
exposure: A state law making fentanyl test strips legal being in force (16 jurisdictions with a dated law, June 2018 to August 2022; implementation dates coded by the authors from a legal database, with the modifications documented in an online appendix)
comparator: The same states before their law and states without such a law at the time (imputation difference-in-differences with state and month fixed effects); for unintentional deaths, also overdose deaths by suicide, homicide or undetermined intent in the same states and months
outcome: Deaths from overdose of any drug (labelled drug-induced deaths in the paper's tables) per 100,000 residents per month, and unintentional drug-overdose deaths; opioid- and fentanyl-specific deaths were not analysed
magnitude: Bhai et al. 2025, Table 3 (log death rate; coefficient and SE clustered by state): whole population −0.069 (0.028) without and −0.074 (0.020) with controls; all races −0.075 (0.030) and −0.078 (0.021); White −0.077 (0.032) and −0.083 (0.023); Black −0.127 (0.028) and −0.088 (0.026). As percentages (the paper's 100(e^β − 1); 95% CI editors' calculation): whole population −6.7% (−11.7% to −1.4%) and −7.1% (−10.7% to −3.4%); White −7.4% and −8.0%; Black −11.9% (the abstract's 13.5% is this value with the sign reversed) and −8.4%. Absolute (editors' rough calculation): about 0.22 fewer deaths per 100,000 residents per month against a mean of 3.03 in state-months with a law, roughly 2.6 to 2.8 per 100,000 a year. Table 4, unintentional against other-intent overdose deaths: whole population −0.053 (0.032) and −0.056 (0.027) (−5.2%, −5.4%); White −0.070 (0.037) and −0.082 (0.031); Black −0.058 (0.029) and −0.002 (0.026; −0.2%, 95% CI −5.2% to +5.0%).

evidence.locator: Results › Primary Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (the 2nd begins on p. 244); Table 2 (p. 245); Table 3 Panels A and B (p. 248)
evidence.extracted: Two-way fixed effects with the Borusyak et al. imputation estimator, log drug-overdose (drug-induced) deaths per 100,000 residents per state-month: test-strip coefficient without controls −0.069 (SE 0.028; p < .05) for the whole population, −0.075 (0.030) all races pooled, −0.077 (0.032) White and −0.127 (0.028; p < .01) Black, which the text gives as reductions of 6.67%, 7.22%, 7.41% and 11.92%; with age, rurality and income controls −0.074 (0.020), −0.078 (0.021), −0.083 (0.023) and −0.088 (0.026), all p < .01; 2,613, 4,181, 2,461 and 1,469 observations. Table 2: mean deaths per 100,000 residents per state-month 3.03 (SD 1.12) with a law and 2.37 (1.12) without. Editors' calculation (100(e^β − 1), 95% CI from β ± 1.96 SE): whole population −6.7% (−11.7% to −1.4%) and −7.1% (−10.7% to −3.4%); White −8.0% and Black −8.4% with controls; applied to 3.03, about 0.22 fewer deaths per 100,000 per month, 2.6 to 2.8 a year.

evidence.locator: Results › Primary Results, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 245); Table 4 Panels A and B (p. 249)
evidence.extracted: Triple differences, unintentional drug-overdose deaths against overdose deaths by suicide, homicide and undetermined intent: without controls −0.053 (SE 0.032; p < .1) whole population, −0.056 (0.033; p < .1) all races, −0.070 (0.037; p < .1) White and −0.058 (0.029; p < .05) Black, all described in the text as statistically significant; with controls −0.056 (0.027; p < .05), −0.061 (0.027; p < .05), −0.082 (0.031; p < .01) and −0.002 (0.026; not significant) for Black residents; 4,455, 5,632, 3,937 and 1,484 observations. Editors' calculation: about 5% to 8% lower relative to the other intents; Black with controls −0.2% (95% CI −5.2% to +5.0%).

evidence.locator: Method › Empirical Strategy, 2nd paragraph (p. 242); Table 1 and note, Figure 1 and note (p. 243)
evidence.extracted: Exposure: an indicator that the state had legalized fentanyl test strips, from the Network for Public Health Law (2024) survey with some dates modified by the authors and details in Online Appendix A. Table 1 gives implementation dates from Maryland 6/1/2018 and Rhode Island 7/2/2018 to Louisiana 8/1/2022 (Colorado, Virginia and the District of Columbia in 2019; Nevada, Delaware, Arizona and Maine in 2021; New Jersey, Wisconsin, Tennessee, West Virginia, Connecticut and North Carolina in 2022). Editors' count and reading of Figure 1: 16 jurisdictions dated (15 states and the District of Columbia), while the map shades 22 as legal as of 2022, adding Alaska, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Vermont and Wyoming without a date.

evidence.locator: Corrigendum p. 299, Changes 1 to 3; pp. 299–300, Change 4; p. 300, Changes 6 and 7 and closing paragraph
evidence.extracted: Corrigendum (2026; doi 10.1177/10775587261457313): the original Methods said Table 1 gave the dates when state legislatures passed statutes legalizing strips, from the Network for Public Health Law (2024); the corrected text says the authors modified some of those dates to represent the policy shock, gives implementation dates and documents the modifications in a new Online Appendix A on the coding of strip legalization. It deletes the Introduction's statements that as of 2024, 21 states and the District of Columbia had legalized strips and that the remaining states treat them as illegal paraphernalia. The journal editor states that the revisions do not alter the results or conclusions.

evidence.locator: Method › Empirical Strategy, 1st paragraph (p. 242) and 8th paragraph (p. 244)
evidence.extracted: Data are monthly state death counts from CDC WONDER for 2018–2022 with population from SEER, analysed as all drug-overdose deaths and as unintentional drug-overdose deaths against those by homicide, suicide and undetermined intent; separate models for White and Black residents and a pooled model adding American Indian or Alaska Native and Asian or Pacific Islander residents; weighted by state population, standard errors clustered by state. The Methods say the two measures capture opioid fatalities likely to be affected by strips, but no ICD-10 codes are given and no opioid- or fentanyl-specific outcome is analysed.

The authors list as limitations state-level data that may hide local variation, possible inconsistencies across states in how overdose deaths are classified or reported, and a study period of only 5 years; they did not measure community groups providing strips, did not consider strip use in states where strips are prohibited, and note that other state policies, including those relevant to hospital administration, may affect overdose deaths.

evidence.locator: Results › Robustness Tests and Sensitivity Analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 245–246); Figures 3 and 4 (pp. 246–247)
evidence.extracted: Event studies from 16 months before to 8 months after the law, without controls (versions with controls said to be not qualitatively different and not shown): the authors report statistically insignificant pre-trends for the whole population, all races and White residents, a sharp reduction almost immediately after legalization, and more volatile results for Black residents because of limited sample size. Editors' reading of the figures (values not extracted): the pre-period 95% bands are much wider than the post-period bands, and for Black residents every pre-period coefficient lies above zero.

evidence.locator: Abstract; New Contributions (p. 241); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 246); Conclusion (p. 248)
evidence.extracted: The abstract reports a 7% decrease for the whole population and a 13.5% reduction among Black individuals, which New Contributions calls nearly twice the White reduction and the Discussion repeats; the Conclusion describes reductions in opioid overdose deaths, particularly among Black populations. Editors' calculation: 13.5% equals 100(e^0.127 − 1), the unadjusted Black coefficient with its sign reversed; correctly converted it is 11.9% (11.92% in the Results), and 8.4% with controls; no opioid-specific outcome was analysed.
evidence.quote: robust evidence that legalizing FTS is associated with significant reductions in opioid overdose deaths

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I serious on the card (sc_bhai_2025): no adjustment for other state policies, federal strip funding from 2021 or changes in each state's drug supply; laws were adopted where death rates were higher; the event-study pre-period intervals are wide; the exposure dates are the authors' modifications, documented only in an appendix not read, and six jurisdictions shaded legal on the map have no date; outcome codes are not given.

inconsistency.note: Single study. Within it, the unintentional-death estimate for Black residents with controls is null (−0.2%), which is stated rather than rated.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: laws and deaths from any drug overdose in US state populations, 2018 to 2022. As evidence on whether using strips prevents deaths it would be indirect (no measure of strip access or use), and it is not cited for that.

imprecision.note: The interval for the main estimate runs from about 1% to 12% fewer deaths without adjustment and 3% to 11% with it (editors' calculation), from a trivial to a sizeable difference; 16 jurisdictions changed law, four of them with at most 7 months of data after it, and clustered standard errors with few treated states can understate uncertainty.

plausible_confounding.note: Remaining confounding could run either way (laws adopted as deaths peaked would favour an apparent fall); no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; it is rated down for risk of bias and for imprecision, which is below the floor, so very low. Worded as an association: a state-level comparison of laws cannot show that the laws, or the strips, caused the lower death rates, and it says nothing about what happened to the people who tested their drugs. Single study: no other study of these laws and deaths was cited by the paper or read.
